what_they_do: 6 of 6 change the picture at least 3 times per 10 s (ranges of 3-5, 4, 4-6, 5-7, 6-10, 8-10), almost always with hard cuts. Our body changes about once per 5-9 s.
6 of 6 bodies are fully moving video (people acting or gesturing, gameplay, CGI, camera pans), not stills. 5 of 6 build it mainly from film, TV or game footage made by others.
6 of 6 narrators are energetic male Hindi voices. 5 of 6 are real human voices and 1 of 6 (4.1M views) sounds synthetic. 3 of 6 show the speaker on camera and 3 of 6 never do.
5 of 6 run continuous background music. 4 of 6 add sound effects through the body (whooshes, impacts, explosions, roars) timed to cuts or action.
Text varies: 2 of 6 use full subtitles, 3 of 6 have none, and 3 of 6 flash large bold labels or cards ('FACT. 2', 'PAUL WALKER', headline cards). 4 of 6 show a surprising visual within the first 3 s.
advice.gap: Every watched video keeps the screen in constant real motion and changes the picture at least 3 times every 10 seconds. Our body holds one still image with a slow zoom for 5-9 seconds, under a quiet music bed with little sound design.

changes.change: Split each narrated scene into 2-3 shots of 2-3 s each and join them with hard cuts, aiming for 3-5 picture changes per 10 s. Build the extra shots from generated variants of the scene: alternate crops, punch-in zooms, a close-up detail, a related insert image. Assemble them automatically with code (ffmpeg or MoviePy) from the script timings.
changes.why: 6 of 6 watched videos change the picture at least 3 times per 10 s. Our body changes about 1-2 times per 10 s.
changes.risk: Needs 2-3x more images per video and more generation cost. Shots that don't match the sentence being spoken will feel random. Cutting too fast can make educational points hard to follow.

changes.change: Replace the static zoom/parallax stills with short AI image-to-video clips of 2-4 s, so the shots have real motion (objects moving, camera moves, people gesturing). Start with the first 3-4 body scenes and the most important ones, then extend if retention improves.
changes.why: 6 of 6 describe constant on-screen motion throughout the body. None of them relies on still images.
changes.risk: AI video artifacts (warped hands, faces, text) can look cheap or uncanny. Generation time and cost grow with every shot. Styles across clips may not stay consistent.

changes.change: Raise the music so it is present rather than quiet, and add a sound-effect layer: a whoosh or pop on every cut, and an impact on each key fact or label. Place these automatically in code at the cut timestamps. Use royalty-free or self-generated sounds.
changes.why: 5 of 6 run continuous background music. 4 of 6 add sound effects through the body; video 2 times whooshes, pops and impacts to its cuts.
changes.risk: Too much sound can drown the narrator or feel gimmicky for learning content. Sound licences must be checked.

changes.change: Make the narrator faster and more energetic. Try expressive settings or a more dynamic AI voice. Also test a voice clone built from the founder's own recorded clips against the current synthetic voice.
changes.why: 6 of 6 narrators deliver energetic, brisk Hindi, and 5 of 6 are real human voices. 1 of 6 (4.1M views) sounds synthetic, so a synthetic voice alone is not disqualifying; energy matters more in these notes.
changes.risk: An over-hyped tone could reduce credibility for a learning channel. A voice clone may sound slightly off, and listeners may find a cloned founder voice misleading if not disclosed.

changes.change: Add large bold keyword or number cards for key terms, facts and numbers ('FACT 2', a key figure), alongside the existing captions. Add short screen recordings the owner makes himself (phone, calculator, apps, websites, diagrams) as motion inserts.
changes.why: 3 of 6 use big bold labels or cards. 3 of 6 use screen recordings or phone-screen close-ups (videos 1, 2, 3). Nothing in the notes shows our captions hurt, so keep them.
changes.risk: Too much text competing with captions can clutter the frame. Screen recordings must not show other creators' content or private data.

do_not: Do not re-cut film, TV, game or streamer footage. 5 of 6 build their body this way, but it copies others' footage, risks copyright strikes and demonetisation, and breaks this channel's rules.

Do not use on-camera roleplay or a presenter visible all the way through. 3 of 6 rely on this (video 1's double-role skit, videos 2 and 3's presenter), but it needs far more than the owner's short opening clip.
Do not present unverified material as real. Video 2 shows 'purported GTA 6 footage', and doing the same would damage trust for a learning channel.
Do not leave signs of reused material on screen. Video 4 shows source subtitles in Chinese, which signals a re-upload.
Do not drop in other people's meme clips or voice snippets. Video 3 ends on an external comedic voice clip and video 1 ends on a meme sound; these carry the same rights problem as borrowed footage.
advice.caveat: This rests on only 6 videos from one week, mostly GTA 6 and fantasy-film recaps rather than learning content, and their views partly reflect creator fame and trending topics, so treat the patterns as hypotheses to A/B test, not proven causes.

what_they_do: The pictures move: 4 of 6 are 100% animated video (AI 3D or Roblox-style 3D) with continuous motion inside the frame. None of the 6 relies mainly on still images. Stills appear only as about 25% of one video and as filmed artwork in another.
Cuts are fast: all 6 of 6 change the picture at least 4 times every 10 seconds (range about 4 to 14), almost always with hard cuts.

The narrator stays unseen and sounds energetic: in 4 of 6 the narrator is never on screen. All 5 of the 5 videos with narration use a dramatic or high-energy storytelling delivery, and 3 of 6 sound openly synthetic or AI.
Sound is continuous and layered: 6 of 6 run music or a vocal track for the whole video plus sound effects matched to what happens on screen (whooshes, impacts, splashes, keyboard clacks).
The first surprising visual comes early: within 2 seconds in 4 of 6 and within 9 seconds in 6 of 6. On-screen text is minimal or absent in 4 of 6, and only 1 of 6 uses big word-by-word captions.
advice.gap: Our body is a series of still pictures, each held for 5-9 seconds with a slow zoom, which works out to roughly 1-2 picture changes per 10 seconds. The watched videos use moving footage that changes 4-14 times per 10 seconds. Our sound is a quiet music bed with no sound effects, while all 6 watched videos keep a loud, continuous score with effects matched to the action.

changes.change: Turn each scene's still into a short AI image-to-video clip (3-5 s) with motion inside the frame: water flowing, fire, a character turning or walking, a camera push. Do this at least for the key beats. Keep stills with parallax only as filler.
changes.why: 4 of 6 are fully moving animation, and 0 of 6 rely mainly on stills.
changes.risk: Higher generation cost and time. Characters may look different from shot to shot, and visual glitches (hands, faces, deity features) can look cheap or cause offence on religious topics. Every clip needs a human check.

changes.change: Cut faster. Split each narrated scene into 2-3 shots, such as a wide shot, a close-up crop, and a reaction or detail image or clip, so the picture changes about every 2-2.5 seconds (about 4-5 cuts per 10 s). Script the shot list automatically from the narration timings.
changes.why: 6 of 6 have at least 4 cuts per 10 seconds, against our 1-2.
changes.risk: If the extra shots don't match what the narrator is saying at that moment, the video feels random rather than fast. It also needs 2-3 times as many generated images.

changes.change: Upgrade the sound. Use a louder, continuous cinematic score under the whole body, and have code place licensed sound effects (whoosh on each cut, plus impact, fire, water or chime sounds matched to the scene content).
changes.why: 6 of 6 have continuous music or chanting plus synced sound effects, while ours has quiet music and no effects.
changes.risk: Music or effects can drown out the narrator. Unlicensed tracks risk copyright claims, so use royalty-free or properly licensed libraries only.

changes.change: Make the narrator more dramatic. Rewrite the script into short, suspenseful sentences with cliffhanger turns, and set the AI voice to a faster, more expressive storytelling style. Keeping a synthetic voice is fine.
changes.why: All 5 of 5 narrated videos use high-energy or dramatic delivery, and 3 of 6 succeed with a voice that sounds openly AI.
changes.risk: The voice can tip into sounding over-acted or tiring. On long 8-14 minute videos, constant intensity may push viewers away.

changes.change: Open the body with its most striking moving visual (the 'impossible' image of the story), and trim the presenter clip toward the short end (about 6 s) so that image arrives sooner.
changes.why: 4 of 6 show a surprising visual within 2 seconds, and 6 of 6 within 9 seconds. Our presenter walk delays the first surprising visual by 6-12 seconds.
changes.risk: A shorter founder clip weakens personal branding. This change touches the opening, not only the body, so test it on a few Shorts first.

do_not: Don't use film or anime clips (Adipurush, the 1992 Ramayana anime) or film other people's artwork off a screen, as 2 of 6 do. It copies others' footage and invites copyright claims.
Don't add a talking head for about 40% of the video (1 of 6) or desk reaction shots (1 of 6). Both need the owner on camera far beyond his short existing clip.
Don't adopt the no-narration format built on screen-recorded Google searches (1 of 6). It depends on filmed reactions and has no voice, which doesn't fit a narrated channel.

Don't copy the blocky Roblox style (2 of 6). It belongs to a kids' fantasy-story niche and would clash with mythology or fact topics. Copying it closely could also look like riding on those creators' look.
Don't remove captions just because 4 of 6 have little text. The notes only show that heavy captions are not required, not that they hurt, and only 1 of 6 uses big word-by-word captions.
advice.caveat: These are 6 of one week's top videos, each watched once with approximate counts, and no low-performing videos were compared, so these traits describe hits but do not prove they cause the views.
